tabStripIconVerification.note: Three tab-search glyph spans, accessible action names, original search scopes, and generated-source drift have focused local checks. The bundled font contains all three ligatures. No new native visual or screen-reader result is claimed.

repairVerification.note: Onboarding preservation, verified-read refusal, configuration preconditions, secret-free receipts, and transient credential cleanup have local regression coverage. Existing captures do not verify these repairs; no new native capture or parity result is claimed.

presentationRepairVerification.note: School mode consumers, runtime-group preservation, queued-speech cancellation and destination-route validation have local regression coverage. No new native capture or design-parity claim is made.

chromeParityBar.what: The reference-versus-built bar a destination in this project can actually meet: outside the regions that carry data, the two artifacts must render identically. Whole-frame pixel identity is unreachable here by deliberate product decision — the design shows invented sample content exactly where the application shows the target's real, usually empty, readings — so 47% to 64% of every frame differs for a reason nobody wants fixed. This bar asks the narrower question instead.
chromeParityBar.whyToleranceIsZero: Both sides are Chromium at the same device metrics reading the same local font files, so identical content can and does produce identical pixels. The committed captures prove that rather than assert it: dash and logger each contain runs of rows that are byte-for-byte equal between the two sides, and inside the credits pill the Roboto digit is byte-for-byte equal on all 32 destinations. A non-zero tolerance would be a number chosen until something passed. QUALIFIED, by measurement taken when statusCell was moved into the compared region: this used to say identical content 'really does produce identical pixels' without qualification, and that is too strong. statusCell renders from one compiled template with nothing overridden on either side, and it still differs by exactly 1420 pixels on every one of the 32 — see chromeParityRun.whatIncludingStatusCellMeasured for the two causes, both of which are real differences between the two artifacts rather than noise. The right reading is that zero is the only defensible tolerance and that meeting it is not free; a tolerance wide enough to absorb those 1420 pixels would also absorb a genuine defect, which is why the figure is reported rather than tolerated. AND THAT IS WHY IT IS REPORTED: those 1420 are now 555. Reporting the figure rather than tolerating it is what made the axis pin findable at all, and chromeParityRun.msymAxisPinDecision records the demonstration and the repair. A tolerance chosen to absorb 1420 pixels would have swallowed the whole defect and nobody would ever have looked.
chromeParityBar.whyThereIsAMinimum: A mask is the one way this bar could be passed without matching anything: widen the declared data regions until nothing is left to compare. The regions declared below leave a little under 30% of a 1440x1000 frame, so a floor of 25% sits below what an honest mask costs and far above what a mask widened to force a pass would leave. compareChrome refuses rather than compares when the floor is breached.
chromeParityBar.howRegionsAreObtained: Measured off both live DOMs by console/scripts/design-parity-regions.mjs during a capture run — never hand-drawn, and never derived from the pixel diff. A mask derived from the diff would exclude exactly what differs and turn every verdict into a match. The shell is located structurally (a three-row layout whose last row is three columns) because the two sides share the design's layout but not its class names, which both toolchains hash at build time.
chromeParityBar.howExclusionsCombine: The exclusion for an area is the union of the two sides' measured rectangles, not their intersection: the sides genuinely disagree about some heights, and an intersection would leave a strip of one side's data inside the compared region and report it as a chrome defect it is not. A union can only ever hide more, which is what the minimum compared fraction and the recorded excluded-region diff are there to keep honest.
chromeParityBar.areaRoleJudgement: The roles below are the one human judgement this bar rests on. They are declared once for the whole application rather than as 32 per-destination masks, so the judgement stays small enough to review and hard to widen quietly.

brandCell.why: The top strip's first cell: the product mark and name. It renders the same thing on every destination and reads nothing from the target. Kept inside the compared region even though it is guaranteed to differ, on the same principle sectionList is: this product's name is one word longer than the design's, so the cell is 6.36px wider — measured, 'Material Asterisk' at 106.63px against 'Asterisk Console' at 100.27px, same 13px/500 Roboto, same 12px padding, 20px glyph and 10px gap — which rounds the two rectangles to 161 and 154. That is a deliberate rename recorded in compile-design.mjs's BRAND table, not a layout defect, and a divergence worth reading in the result rather than hiding in a mask.

menuCell.why: The top strip's menu bar — a fixed set of menu titles, identical on every destination. Its 12.28% divergence, also identical on every destination, is not its own: it is the 7px the brand cell beside it takes, displacing every glyph in this cell by exactly that much. The figure read 12.00% while commandCell was still compared, on the same 1886 differing pixels; reclassifying commandCell as data clipped nine columns of matching pixels off this cell's compared strip, which raised the ratio without changing a single pixel of the artifact.

commandCell.why: The top strip's connection pill, and DECIDED: it is data. It renders connLabel and connUptime, which are this.target.label and this.target.detail — what the console's own discovery reports about the target it found: 'no target' / 'nothing discovered yet' with none configured, or the discovered distribution name and 'N local target(s), connection verified' once one answers. The design invents 'pbx-hq · AMI 5038' and 'up 14d 06:22' in the same two spans. That is this bar's founding sentence exactly — the design shows invented sample content where the application shows a real reading — so the cell is data in the same sense contentPane is, and the previous declaration's 'carries its own label, not a reading' was simply false. It is NOT the brandCell or sectionList case. Those two are also guaranteed to differ and are deliberately still compared, because they differ where this product renders different CHROME from the design's chrome: a product name one word longer, a per-row badge this application removed. Reporting that is what the bar is for. This cell differs because the design invented a reading, which is what the bar is for excluding. What the decision costs, measured rather than predicted: the compared fraction falls from exactly 29.5717% to exactly 28.0883% of the frame — 404472 pixels of 1440000, above the declared 25% floor — and the compared-region divergence falls from 6.34%-14.95% to 4.62%-13.68%. What it also hides, said plainly: the region probe measures cells and not text runs, so excluding this rectangle also excludes the pill's own border, radius, pulse dot and separator, which are chrome. 61.00% of the cell already matched, so most of what the mask now covers is pixels that agreed, and excluded.diffPercentage goes on reporting whatever it covers — 29.76% to 81.88% across the 32, against 29.56% to 82.79% before. Two measured results contradicted what was expected of this move and are recorded because they did. FIRST, removing the worst area did not leave one uniform worst area behind it: the worst compared area is now brandCell on 21 destinations, tabStrip on 7 and sectionList on 4, where before it was this cell on all 32. The single identical figure was hiding a spread. SECOND, menuCell's divergence ROSE, from 12.00% to 12.28%, without one new differing pixel — its differing count is 1886 before and after. Union rectangles overlap, so excluding this cell also clipped nine columns off menuCell's compared strip, and all 360 of those pixels matched. Excluding an area can raise a neighbour's reported percentage by removing agreement rather than by finding disagreement, and a reading of these numbers that misses that will attribute a rise to a regression.

statusCell.why: The top strip's last cell, and DECIDED: it is chrome. Its previous declaration read 'carries live status: what the console is connected to and how that connection is faring', and that sentence describes commandCell rather than this cell; a pass corrected the text and deliberately left the role alone so that this move could be measured on its own. The fourth top cell is the Beginner/Expert mode picker, the confirmation-credits pill, the command-palette button and the three window controls. The decisive evidence is not the description but the renderer: App.tsx overrides exactly two values in the whole top strip, connLabel and connUptime, and both of them land in commandCell. Nothing inside this cell is written by the product at all — both sides render the same modeOpts, the same credits count, the same search glyph and the same three window buttons out of the same compiled template — so there is no invented reading here for the bar to exclude, and excluding it was a narrowing nobody had argued for. What the decision costs, measured rather than predicted: the compared fraction RISES from exactly 28.0883% to exactly 29.1106% of the frame — 419192 pixels of 1440000, the 404472 that were compared before plus this cell's own 14720 — which is the first move of an area that widened the comparison rather than narrowing it. The compared-region divergence moves from 4.62%-13.68% to 4.80%-13.54%: the low end rises and the high end falls, because this cell diverges by more than the least-divergent destinations did and by less than the most-divergent ones. No neighbouring area's figure moved at all, unlike the commandCell move, because this cell's union rectangle is 1072-1440 and touches nothing else's. And what it revealed is the thing worth having done it for: see chromeParityRun.whatIncludingStatusCellMeasured.

tabStrip.why: The open-tab strip. Tab titles come from the navigation catalogue, which is itself compiled from the design, so both sides are naming the same screens.

rail.why: The navigation rail: six fixed rail icons and their labels, compiled from the design's own catalogue. Chrome deliberately — a divergence here is a real layout defect and the bar is supposed to report it rather than excuse it.

sectionList.why: The section list for the open rail. Kept inside the compared region on purpose even though this application removed the design's per-row badges: the labels are chrome, and a badge present on one side and absent on the other is a divergence worth reading in the result rather than one worth hiding in a mask.

contentPane.why: The destination's own screen. This is where the design's invented rows, dashboard tiles, health bars and history sit, and where the built application puts the target's real readings instead. It is the region this bar exists to exclude.

compiledEvidence.method: compile-then-render: console/scripts/compile-design.mjs compiles design/Asterisk Console M3.dc.html and design/M3 Control.dc.html into app/renderer/src/generated/{console.tsx,m3-control.tsx,design-styles.css,design-manifest.json}, which console/app/renderer/src/App.tsx subclasses directly rather than a hand-matched reimplementation.
compiledEvidence.coverage: Renders all 32 destinations from the generated design model and asserts each one's design title, description, owning source file (Expert mode), its control groups (including the design M3 control's slider/stepper/order affordances), Beginner-mode plain wording, and all 17 transient-state overlay families.

captureContract.status: captures, diffs, region ledgers and chrome-parity records now exist for ALL 32 audited destinations, About included, and are committed. Every one came from a single pass per side against one build of this tree, so each destination's rectangles and its pixels are the same moment of the same render. All 32 rows nevertheless remain compiled, none verified — see chromeParityRun for what the bar measures now, and geometryDivergence for what was repaired to get there
captureContract.closedGap: design/support.js loads React itself (loadReactUmd) from unpkg, and reads window.__resources[url] first (cdnScriptFor), so the design already ships the host hook. console/scripts/vendor-design-react-host.mjs vendors react/react-dom 18.3.1 into console/design-reference/vendor/, verified against the sha384 subresource-integrity hashes design/support.js itself declares, and the capture host sets that map. Nothing under design/ is edited and a capture run makes no network request.
captureContract.builtRouteStatus: ding-pbx:// is now a route the application resolves, not a template only. console/shared/destination-route.ts is the one place it is spelled, parsed and refused; app/electron/main.ts registers the scheme, takes the single-instance lock, reads it off the launch command line and off a second-instance activation, and holds it until the renderer has loaded; app/renderer/src/App.tsx resolves the id against the compiled catalogue and calls the shell's own openScreen. The application acts on the destination alone: state, theme, width, height and scale are validated so a malformed route is refused whole, and are deliberately not applied, because a link that resized a window or flipped a theme would be a link that edited somebody's settings. The committed built captures were NOT retaken through the route -- they remain the ones the run below recorded, driven to each destination through the same rail-then-section clicks the reference side performs.
captureContract.destinationRouteMapping: Every destination row carries its final referenceRoute, builtRoute and builtCapture rather than leaving all three to be re-derived from evidenceTemplates by whoever needs them. The routes are checked against the templates AND the builtRoute is parsed by the product's own parser and required to resolve to that row's own id, so a row cannot name a route the application would refuse or one that opens a different screen.

captureRun.diffPercentageRange: 23.07% to 60.98% of pixels differ, down from 47.13% to 63.95% before the two capture-harness repairs recorded in geometryDivergence

captureRun.areTheThirtyOneBuiltCapturesStale: No, and the question is worth answering rather than leaving to inference, because the commit that removed the About heading divergence edited App.tsx's renderVals, which every destination renders through. The edit is confined to the 'about' screen: for every other screen the composed subheading is character-for-character what it was, and the removed screenTitle override only ever fired on 'about'. So the thirty-one committed built captures still show what this commit's renderer draws. compareCaptures' own staleness check compares file mtimes, which a fresh clone does not preserve, so it would not have caught this either way.

captureRun.whyNothingWasVerifiedUnderTheOldBar: verifyDesignParityEvidence requires a 'match' verdict, and compareCaptures calls a match only when the two captures are pixel-identical. That bar is unreachable here BY DELIBERATE PRODUCT DECISION, not by a defect in the harness: this project removed the design's sample rows, dashboard tiles, health bars, nav badges, history, agent rail and trunk-authentication content from the running application, so the reference shows invented content where the built application shows the target's real (often empty) readings. The diffs measure that divergence rather than a rendering fault — none of the 31 was refused as unpainted or stale, and the side-by-side images show identical chrome beside different data. Moving a row to 'verified' therefore needs a parity bar that compares chrome and layout with the data-bearing regions excluded, plus a real Material Design 3 conformance audit per destination; neither existed when this was written. SUPERSEDED IN FULL: the parity bar half now exists — see chromeParityRun — and so does the Material Design 3 half, see materialAuditRun. The objection that a generated audit nobody performed would be an invented verdict still stands, and is what shaped the auditor rather than what prevented it: its conforms value is computed from what it measured and cannot be supplied by a caller, so it can only ever report a divergence it actually found. It reports all 32 destinations nonconforming.

chromeParityRun.whatChanged: verifyDesignParityEvidence no longer asks the whole-frame visualDiff for a 'match'. A verified row now rests on the chrome-parity bar declared in chromeParityBar above: outside the regions measured as data-bearing, the two artifacts must render identically at tolerance 0. The whole-frame diff is still required and still read — it is the record of how far the data diverges — but it is now required to be a real comparison rather than a match, and a 'refused' one is refused exactly as before.
chromeParityRun.howTheRegionsWereMeasured: One full run per side. Each destination's rectangles were measured on the live DOM while that screen was settled and before anything else touched it, in the same loop iteration that photographed it — so the mask and the pixels are the same render rather than two visits that happen to agree. CHANGED when the .msym axis pin was removed, and the change is a repair rather than a convenience: both sides now run under the SAME Chromium — Electron 43.4.1, headed, on an off-screen Windows desktop created by scripts/launch-on-hidden-desktop.ps1 — where the reference side previously ran under headless Edge while only the built side ran under Electron. Two artifacts compared at a tolerance of exactly zero were being rendered by two different browsers in two different modes. msymAxisPinDecision measures what that was worth: retaking the reference side alone, with no change to the product at all, RAISES the navigation rail's divergence on every one of the 32. The reference side still runs with a capture run's full request interception, and still reached no network — 710 requests to the capture host, 64 font stylesheets answered locally, 0 blocked. This supersedes the previous two --regions-only runs, which existed so the bar could be applied to captures that were already committed, and which left the rectangles and the pixels a run apart.

chromeParityRun.chromeDiffRange: 2.95% to 12.20% of the compared region differs, across six compared areas. It was 4.80% to 13.54% before the .msym axis pin was removed and both sides were retaken under one browser, and before that 4.62% to 13.68% while statusCell was still excluded, 6.34% to 14.95% while commandCell was still compared, and 6.67% to 26.78% before the harness repairs. THIS movement is not like the earlier ones and the difference matters: every previous change to this figure came from reclassifying an area while the same 64 committed PNGs went in, so nothing about either artifact had moved. This one comes from a changed product and 64 new PNGs. See msymAxisPinDecision for how much of it belongs to the product and how much to the harness, measured rather than apportioned by argument.
chromeParityRun.comparedFractionRange: exactly 29.1106% of the frame is compared on every one of the 32 — 419192 pixels of 1440000 — against a declared floor of 25%. UNCHANGED by the axis-pin removal and the two-sided retake, which is itself worth reading: the compared fraction is a property of the declared roles and the measured rectangles, and neither moved, so the divergence figures above and below can be compared with the ones they replaced. It was exactly 28.0883% while statusCell was excluded, exactly 29.5717% before commandCell was reclassified as data, and ranged 29.5% to 29.6% before the harness repairs made five of the eight areas measure the same rectangle on both sides.
chromeParityRun.whatIncludingStatusCellMeasured: The reason this move was worth making, and it is not the compared fraction. statusCell was expected to match: both sides draw it from one compiled template, App.tsx overrides nothing inside it, and the region probe measures the identical rectangle 1072,0,368,40 on both sides of all 32. It does not match. It differs by exactly 1420 of its 14720 pixels — 9.6467% — with the SAME count on every one of the 32, which is the signature of one cause rather than 32. Measuring where those 1420 sit gives two causes, and neither is noise. FIRST, THE ICON GLYPHS. Every differing pixel outside the mode picker sits on a Material Symbols glyph: the credits pill's confirmation_number at columns 1237-1259 (129 differing), the command-palette search glyph at 1302-1317 (119), and the three window controls remove/crop_square/close at 1345-1356, 1379-1390 and 1413-1424 (46, 88 and 84). The discriminator is in the same pill: the Roboto digit beside that icon, columns 1267-1284, is byte-for-byte IDENTICAL — 0 differing pixels. Roboto matches and Material Symbols does not, in adjacent runs of the same control, so this is not antialiasing in general. Both sides are served the same local material-symbols-outlined-100-700-0.woff2 — the reference side through the capture run's font interception, which answers fonts.googleapis.com out of console/assets/fonts. What differs is the rule: font-variation-settings appears ZERO times anywhere under design/ and exactly ONCE in the built renderer, in the .msym rule compile-design.mjs adds, pinning FILL 0, wght 400, GRAD 0 and opsz 24. Material Symbols Outlined is a variable font whose axes the design's own stylesheet link requests as opsz 20..48, wght 100..700, FILL 0..1, GRAD -50..200, so the built side draws every icon from a pinned instance and the reference side draws it from the file's default instance. SECOND, THE PICKER'S BORDER. 548 of the 946 pixels differing inside the mode picker are in five rows, and they are the box's own 1px border rather than anything inside it: on the reference the top border is a single crisp row 6 at rgb(65,73,66) with rows 5 and 34 pure background, while on the built side the same ink is split across rows 5 and 6 at rgb(24,31,25) and rgb(40,52,45), and the same at the bottom. The built side draws the 28px-tall picker box half a pixel higher. That is a real sub-pixel layout difference and it is NOT a whole-frame offset: shifting the built region by -2, -1, +1 or +2 pixels raises the divergence in every run rather than lowering it, so dx=0 is already the best alignment, and the Roboto digit above proves at least one glyph is at exactly the same subpixel position on both sides.
chromeParityRun.whatWhatIncludingStatusCellMeasuredDoesN: SUPERSEDED BY msymAxisPinDecision, and it is worth saying which half of it survived. This read: the icon cause is measured to its mechanism but not demonstrated, because that pass did not re-render either side with the axes changed; and the picker-border cause is measured to its symptom only, with its origin unknown. The icon half has now been demonstrated, the pin has been removed, and statusCell falls from 1420 differing pixels to 555 on every one of the 32. The picker-border half turned out not to be a product divergence at all: with both sides rendered by the same browser, no pixel in the picker's border rows differs, and the 555 that remain are entirely in the text band, rows 14 to 25. So the first cause was real and is repaired; the second was an artifact of comparing two different browsers and is gone with them.
chromeParityRun.msymAxisPinDecision: THE DECISION: the compiler no longer pins the Material Symbols variation axes, and the pin's removal is demonstrated rather than argued. WHAT THE PIN WAS. compile-design.mjs appended font-variation-settings:"FILL" 0,"wght" 400,"GRAD" 0,"opsz" 24 to its own .msym rule from its first commit, 9beed2f159 — which is thirty minutes BEFORE the 49-face font download in 0611732d0, and the line was never touched again. The roadmap item that raised this worried that the pin had arrived with that download and that removing it might undo a repair; the ordering disproves the premise. It is Google's own documented Material Symbols snippet, carried in unchanged. WHAT IT DID, MEASURED. scripts/woff2-fvar.mjs reads the shipped face's own fvar table: four axes, defaulting to FILL 0, GRAD 0, opsz 24 and wght 400. Three of the four pinned values were the file's own defaults and did nothing at all. The fourth did a great deal — CSS font-optical-sizing defaults to auto, which drives opsz from the used font-size, and font-variation-settings outranks it, so a fixed opsz 24 replaced every icon's own optical size with a 24px icon's. The design draws 175 icons and four of them are 24px. THE DEMONSTRATION. scripts/design-parity-msym-axes.mjs renders all 98 distinct literal (size, ligature) pairs the design draws, four ways, in one Chromium at this capture tuple's metrics, from the shipped font file: 95 of the 98 differ under the pin and 11252 pixels change, the three that do not are exactly the 24px ones, pinning opsz per icon at clamp(font-size, 20, 48) instead reproduces the design's own rendering to ZERO differing pixels across the whole frame, and with the pin gone the shipped .msym rules draw the design's icons to zero differing pixels. THE FOUR-WAY ISOLATION, and the part worth reading twice. This pass changed two things — the product, and the harness, which now renders both sides under one browser instead of headless Edge against headed Electron. scripts/design-parity-msym-destination.mjs separates them across all 32 destinations by comparing both reference sets against both built sets. On the navigation rail: baseline 2401-6676 differing pixels, pin removed alone 3346-7432, reference retaken alone 4457-8574, both together 0-4411 with an exact zero on 12 destinations. EITHER CHANGE ALONE MAKES IT WORSE ON EVERY DESTINATION BUT ONE, AND ONLY BOTH TOGETHER CONVERGE. A pass that had removed the pin and kept the committed reference captures would have measured a correct repair as a regression, and would very reasonably have backed it out. The single exception is codecs, where removing the pin alone does lower the rail figure, and it is named rather than absorbed into a 'most destinations'. WHAT IT COST AND BOUGHT. statusCell 1420 to 555 on all 32; brandCell 1002 to 846; the rail byte-identical on 12 of 32 where it was never below 2401; the compared-region divergence 4.80%-13.54% to 2.95%-12.20%; the compared fraction unchanged at exactly 29.1106%; the worst-area tally unchanged at brandCell 21, tabStrip 7, sectionList 4. menuCell moved 1886 to 1888, which is the control: it holds no icon, its divergence is the 7px the product rename displaces, and it was expected not to move.
chromeParityRun.whatMsymAxisPinDecisionDoesNotClaim: No destination moved to verified and none could: all 32 still report a real chrome divergence and the Material Design 3 audit still reports all 32 nonconforming. The 555 pixels still differing in statusCell are not explained — they sit in the mode picker's text band, in three column runs matching the check glyph and the two labels, and nothing here says why. The rail's remaining divergence on 20 of the 32 is likewise unexplained; it is 0 or 1 on seven of the eight pbx-rail destinations and larger elsewhere, and no cause was established. The reference and built runs are one full pass each, taken in one session against one build of this tree, but master gained an IAX2 destination and a further screen repair after that build, and this branch re-photographs neither. Captures and a branch that keeps merging a moving default branch cannot both be current; what is guaranteed is that every figure came from one build, and that build is named. And the browser change repairs a real mismatch without making the two sides identical machines: they are one Chromium build in one mode, which is a stronger claim than before and still not a proof that every remaining pixel belongs to the artifacts. SUPERSEDED IN ONE PART, and the sentence above is left standing because it was true when it was written: the 555 pixels ARE explained now, see statusCellTextDecision below. The rail's remaining divergence on 20 of the 32 is still unexplained.
chromeParityRun.statusCellTextDecision: Where the mode picker's half pixel enters: it is a third of a pixel, it is a font weight rather than a box offset, and it enters through a default nobody chose in the design. The built application draws the INACTIVE mode button one weight step heavier than the design does. Nothing in the markup says so -- the button declares font:inherit and no weight of its own on both sides -- but App.tsx's appearance system writes its own default font-weight 500 onto the shell root at startup (currentAppearanceValues' str('ap_weight', '500'), applied by applyAppearanceToDom), so every element that inherits its weight renders at 500. The design declares the same 500 default for the same control and feeds it only to the Appearance screen's preview swatch. `Expert` is the only text in this cell that inherits its weight, which is why every other glyph here is byte-identical. At 500 that label measures 0.359375px wider, so the picker measures 0.359375px wider; the status group is packed against the right edge of the strip, so the picker's RIGHT edge is pinned and its LEFT edge moves, taking the check glyph and both labels with it, while the credits pill outside it does not move at all. Every one of those rectangles still rounds to the same painted device pixel -- 1072.09375 and 1071.734375 both paint at 1072 -- because Chromium snaps a painted box to whole device pixels and positions text at sub-pixel precision, which is exactly why reading the boxes could never have found this and why the offset appeared to have no source. Demonstrated rather than argued: rendering the checked-in design as the top-level document and applying the four declarations applyAppearanceToDom writes reproduces the committed BUILT capture's statusCell to ZERO differing pixels, while the same render untouched reproduces the committed REFERENCE capture's statusCell to zero. Both frames are committed, so the whole claim re-derives from committed bytes with no browser. Two hypotheses were falsified on the way and are recorded so nobody pays for them twice: the capture harness's iframe-inside-transform wrapper contributes zero pixels here, and replacing the design runtime's sc-interp span wrappers with the bare text nodes the compiled renderer emits changes no rectangle and no pixel. console/docs/evidence/statuscell-text-pixels.md.
chromeParityRun.whatStatusCellTextDecisionDoesNotClaim: Nothing is repaired. The default is still 500 and the built application still renders every inheriting weight one step heavier than the design draws it; changing that would move type across every screen and invalidate all 64 committed captures, which is a product decision rather than a measurement. This measures statusCell only: the same root declaration reaches every inheriting weight in the frame, applyAppearanceToDom writes three more declarations beside it -- a colour, a family and a size -- and how much of the other seven areas they account for is not measured. No destination moved to verified and none could; all 32 still report a real chrome divergence and the Material Design 3 audit still reports all 32 nonconforming. No destination capture was retaken: the two reproduction frames are new and the 64 destination captures are the ones the axis-pin run took.
chromeParityRun.whatTheWorstAreaTallyChanged: It was {commandCell: 32}. One area being worst on every single destination, at an identical 39.00%, was the signature of a single cause — the design's invented connection reading against the application's real one — and excluding it did not leave a second uniform worst area behind. It left a spread across three areas, which is what the tally now shows. Also worth reading carefully: menuCell's divergence rose from 12.00% to 12.28% with no new differing pixel, because the excluded union rectangle overlaps it by nine columns of matching pixels. An area's percentage can rise when a neighbour is excluded. UNCHANGED by admitting statusCell: the tally is still {brandCell: 21, tabStrip: 7, sectionList: 4}, because statusCell's 9.65% is below brandCell's 15.56% everywhere, so it is worst on nothing. And no other area's figure moved by a single pixel this time — statusCell's union spans 1072 to 1440 and overlaps no other compared area, so unlike the commandCell move there was no neighbour to clip.

perAreaDivergence.rail: 0.0000% to 5.4366%, byte-identical on 12 of the 32; was 2.9592% to 8.2282% and never zero

chromeParityRun.howToReadPerAreaDivergence: Three of the six are identical to four decimal places on every destination and three vary. That split is the useful signal in this table rather than the figures themselves: an area whose divergence does not move across 32 different screens is not diverging because of the screen, so its cause is one thing and can be named — the product rename for brandCell, the 7px that rename displaces for menuCell, and what msymAxisPinDecision measured for statusCell. The three that vary are diverging because of what is on the screen, which is the content difference this project made on purpose. TWO THINGS TO READ IN THE NEW FIGURES. The rail reaching exactly 0 on 12 destinations is the strongest single result in this table: it is 81136 compared pixels of nothing but icons and their labels, it was never below 2401 before, and a zero standing beside non-zeros for the same area on other destinations is what proves the comparison is live rather than vacuously empty. And menuCell moving by two pixels while everything around it moved by hundreds is the control working: it carries no icon, so the axis pin could not reach it.
chromeParityRun.whyNothingIsVerifiedYet: Two things, and neither is a defect in the bar. FIRST, no destination meets it: every one of the 31 reports a real chrome divergence, so the bar is doing its job rather than waving them through. SECOND, a verified row still needs the per-destination Material Design 3 conformance audit. SUPERSEDED IN PART: that audit has now been performed and committed for all 32 destinations — see materialAuditRun below — and it reports every one of them nonconforming. It is therefore now a second measured reason nothing is verified, rather than an absent prerequisite.
chromeParityRun.theOneDivergenceUnderneathMostOfIt: SUPERSEDED, AND ITS ATTRIBUTION WAS WRONG. It read: brandCell differs by exactly 15.6% and menuCell by exactly 12.0% on every destination, and the cause is that the reference shell is 1428 wide on 20 of the 32 while the built shell is 1440. The identical-figures reasoning was right and the cause was not — those two areas diverged by the same amount on the eleven destinations where the reference shell was a full 1440 wide too, so a scrollbar cannot have been what moved them. Three separate causes were measured instead, and geometryDivergence records each one, what it was repaired in, and what it left behind.
chromeParityRun.supersededBy: materialAuditRun, for the Material Design 3 half of whyNothingIsVerifiedYet only. Nothing else in this section changed.
chromeParityRun.whatCouldStillBeWrongWithThisEvidence: Two of the three limitations recorded here are gone and one is not. GONE: the rectangles and the pixels no longer come from different runs — each destination was measured and photographed in the same loop iteration, on both sides. GONE: the built artifact's commit is identified — console/dist and console/dist-electron were built from this tree, and console/resources/update-manifest.json records that candidate commit in the same change as these captures. STILL TRUE: compareChrome's staleness check compares each built capture's mtime against the build output's mtimes, and a checkout stamps every file with the time it was written, so in any run made from a fresh linked worktree that check compares 'the checkout happened after the build', which was never in doubt. Treat the 32 passes as an absence of contrary evidence rather than as proof, and rely on the single-pass provenance above instead, which does not depend on a timestamp at all. ADDED BY THE statusCell RE-RUN, because it is a limitation that pass created rather than found: that re-run's staleness check walked console/dist ONLY — 21 files, the Vite renderer output the built captures actually photographed — and not console/dist-electron. The recorded newestBuildSourceMtimeMs is unchanged at 1787691669082.8162, because that figure has always come from dist and it is the same figure the records this re-run replaced already carried. The reason dist-electron was absent is a mistake worth writing down rather than tidying away: the pass reached the capture-provenance build output through a directory junction, and a routine `npx tsc -b` then wrote through that junction and restamped all 93 files of console/dist-electron in the linked worktree holding it, from about 1787691669000 to 1787697942397. Nothing tracked was touched and the directory is ignored build output a rebuild restores, but its mtimes are no longer the ones the captures were taken beside, so including it would have made every record refuse on a staleness the pass had itself manufactured. Excluding it narrows what this particular check considered from 114 files to 21. It does not change what the check concluded, and the honest reading is that this run's timestamp provenance is one directory weaker than the run it replaced.

geometryDivergence.question: The roadmap asked where the shell-geometry divergence gets repaired: in the application, in the design, or in the capture harness. The answer is the capture harness, twice, and the third thing was never geometry.
geometryDivergence.whatWasActuallyMeasured: Before the repairs, five of the eight declared areas diverged on every destination and every height diverged. After them, statusCell, tabStrip, rail, sectionList and contentPane measure the SAME rectangle on both sides on all 32 destinations, and the only remaining geometric difference is three top-strip cells moved by one number.

causeOne.what: The reference document was never given the height its own root style needs.
causeOne.evidence: The design's root element is 'height:100%; overflow:hidden' — the same shape the built application's shell has. A percentage height against an auto-height body computes to auto, so the shell grew to its content: 622px to 7668px tall across the 32, and 1428px wide on 20 of them because the document then scrolled. design/support.js supplies exactly the missing stylesheet in its own FULL_PAGE_CSS constant, but only 'if (!parsed.preview)', and this export declares a $preview of 1440x900 in its data-props — so the runtime withholds it and leaves the sizing to the frame the design tool would have provided. Served bare in an iframe, nothing provided it.
causeOne.repairedIn: the capture harness — console/scripts/design-parity-server.mjs injectFullPageHeight, which serves that exact stylesheet with the hosted design, read out of support.js's own declaration rather than typed. Nothing under design/ is edited, on disk or in flight.
causeOne.effect: All 32 reference shells are now exactly 1440x1000 at the window origin, matching the built side. No scrollbar, no content-driven growth.

causeTwo.what: Every built capture was taken behind the update banner.
causeTwo.evidence: The banner is raised by the updater's own background check, which completes whenever it completes — not at startup — and the driver dismissed once, before the first destination. A full 32-destination run was taken with it up: the application's shell sat at (0,43) on the first twenty-two destinations and (0,52) on the last ten, as the banner's text rewrapped for a newer version. Nothing failed and the captures looked entirely normal. The committed built regions from the previous pass do not show this, so the surface arrived between the two runs.
causeTwo.repairedIn: the capture harness — clearUpdateBanner, which dismisses and PROVES dismissed before every destination rather than once, in the shape the onboarding-wizard dismissal already had; plus a general refusal when a built measurement's shell does not sit at the window origin, which names whatever is above it. The second guard is not about the banner: it catches any surface that displaces the shell, including one nobody has thought of.
causeTwo.effect: All 32 built shells are now exactly 1440x1000 at the window origin.

causeThree.what: The brand cell is 7px wider in the application, and it is not geometry.
causeThree.evidence: 'Material Asterisk' measures 106.63px where the design's 'Asterisk Console' measures 100.27px, at the same 13px/500 Roboto inside the same 12px padding, 20px glyph and 10px gap: 154.27px against 160.63px, rounding to 154 and 161. Every remaining top-strip displacement is that one number — menuCell moves right by 7 and commandCell is squeezed by 8.
causeThree.repairedIn: nowhere, and that is the finding. It is a deliberate product rename recorded in compile-design.mjs's BRAND table and in console/design/inventory.json under source.sanitization, of the same kind as the sample data this project removed. It is not repaired in the application because the name is the product's own; not in the design, which is the reference and is never edited; and not in the harness, which is reporting it correctly.
causeThree.effect: brandCell differs by 15.56% and menuCell by 12.28% on every one of the 32, permanently, and both stay inside the compared region so the divergence is read rather than masked. menuCell's figure was 12.00% while commandCell was still compared; the same 1886 pixels differ either way, and the ratio moved only because reclassifying commandCell as data clipped nine columns of matching pixels off menuCell's compared strip.

geometryDivergence.whatThisDidNotDo: No destination moved to verified and none could. Every one of the 32 still reports a real chrome divergence, and the Material Design 3 audit still reports all 32 nonconforming. What changed is that the chrome numbers now measure the product's real differences from the design rather than two defects in the equipment measuring them.

materialAuditRun.whatChanged: The per-destination Material Design 3 conformance audit the verified guard requires has been performed and committed for all 32 audited destinations. Every prior note in this file saying no materialAudit file had been generated is superseded by this section; the reason those notes gave was right and still is, which is why the audit is a measurement rather than a written verdict.
materialAuditRun.whyAMachineMayWriteThisOneAfterAll: The objection recorded for several passes — that a generated audit nobody performed would be an invented verdict — is aimed at exactly one construction: a script that writes conforms:true without looking. auditMaterial is the opposite construction. `conforms` is computed as `defects.length === 0` from findings derived out of the rendered markup, there is no argument, option or code path that can set it, and a caller passing conforms:true is ignored — negative-design-parity-material.mjs plants that exact attempt and requires it to be refused. Every check here can only ever ADD a defect, so a check that fails to fire understates the divergence and none can manufacture a conformance. The direction of error is the point.
materialAuditRun.whatWasAudited: The built product renderer — console/app/renderer/src/App.tsx, the class the application actually mounts — rendered at each destination, together with the effective stylesheet the built renderer loads (app/renderer/src/styles.css and the generated design-styles.css it imports). Not the bare compiled shell App subclasses, and not the design export: the conformance question a verified row asks is about the chrome a person operates.

checks.typeScale: every explicit font-size must be one of the 15 Material Design 3 type-scale sizes
checks.iconSize: every icon glyph must be drawn at one of the 4 Material Design 3 icon sizes
checks.shapeScale: every corner radius must be one of the 6 shape-scale steps, or fully rounded
checks.elevation: a shadow must be a two-layer Material Design 3 elevation, not a single custom layer
checks.stateLayer: hover and pressed must be a translucent state layer over the existing surface rather than an opaque colour swap, and a focus state must exist
checks.touchTarget: an interactive element must reach the 48dp minimum in both axes
checks.motion: durations and easing curves must be Material Design 3 motion tokens

materialAuditRun.theShapeOfWhatItFound: The design is a design-tool export whose measurements were chosen by eye rather than taken from the scale, and the audit says so in exact numbers rather than in adjectives. Type sizes land on 11.5, 12.5, 13, 13.5, 14.5, 15, 15.5, 18, 20 and 54px, none of which the type scale contains; icon glyphs on 14 through 22, 30, 32 and 34px against a scale of 20/24/40/48; radii on 5, 7, 9, 10, 14, 18, 20, 24 and 26px against 0/4/8/12/16/28. Every interaction state is an opaque colour swap rather than a state layer. Every shadow is a single custom layer rather than a two-layer elevation. Durations sit at 120, 160, 180, 220, 240, 280, 320, 340 and 360ms against a token set that has 100, 150, 200, 250, 300 and 350.
materialAuditRun.whatItFoundConforming: Not nothing, and this matters because an auditor that reported everything as wrong would be exactly as useless as one that reported everything as right. cubic-bezier(.2,0,0,1) — the curve most of this interface transitions on — IS the Material Design 3 standard easing token and is not reported; the two curves that are reported are overshoot springs. Icon glyphs at 20px and 24px pass. Radii at 8, 12, 16 and 999px pass. The application's own stylesheet declares focus states, so the focus half of the state-layer check does not fire. The auditor's tests additionally hold it against a fully conformant synthetic screen and require a clean verdict.
materialAuditRun.whatThisAuditDoesNotClaim: It reads declarations, not pixels. It cannot decide whether a control whose measurements are correct is a real Material Design 3 component or a custom lookalike sharing its numbers; it cannot see geometry that only exists after layout, so a flex child that declares no size is not held to the touch-target minimum; it cannot see a style injected at runtime; it cannot watch motion actually run; and it measures no colour tokens at all, so nothing here says whether a hard-coded colour is the colour role its position calls for. Every record repeats these five limits in its own notMeasured field so the limit travels with the verdict. Closing them needs the same driven-build route the captures use.
materialAuditRun.freshness: `--check` re-derives all 32 records from the current renderer and fails if a committed one would differ or is missing. It runs in npm run test:inventories, so a renderer change that moves a screen without re-auditing it turns the suite red rather than leaving a verdict about a screen nobody can reach.
materialAuditRun.theOneDefectThisPassFoundInItself: The freshness comparison originally compared the record bytes exactly as read. This checkout runs with core.autocrlf=true, so a record written with LF is materialised with CRLF in every other checkout of the same commit, and the check was therefore green only on the machine that wrote the records. It was found by running the suite in the primary checkout after merging: the identical commit that had just passed in the linked working tree reported all 32 records stale. Both sides now have carriage returns stripped before comparing, and both directions are planted in the red-then-green proof and in the tests: a CRLF record must not be reported stale, and stripping carriage returns must not blind the check to a real edit. Worth recording rather than quietly fixing, because green-where-written and red-everywhere-else is the worst direction for a freshness check to be wrong in, and the ordinary single-tree run cannot see it.
